drills.q: Why does Amazon's PR/FAQ format start with a press release before implementation detail?
drills.a: Writing the announcement first forces the author to state the customer-facing value proposition in plain language before getting lost in detail -- if it can't be stated clearly, that's an early, cheap warning sign, not a late, expensive one.

drills.q: Name the four roles in a stakeholder map for moving a decision you don't own.
drills.a: Decider (whose yes actually counts), Approver/Blocker (can green-light or veto a piece), Allies (amplify with minimal convincing), Skeptics (need real evidence).

drills.q: What's the correct order to pre-wire stakeholders before a group decision meeting, and why does Skeptics come before Approvers/Blockers?
drills.a: Allies first (cheap feedback, sharpens the pitch), then Skeptics in 1:1s, then Approvers/Blockers, then the Decider. Skeptics come early because their objection raised privately is a gift you can address before it costs credibility live in the room.

drills.q: A proposal justifies itself purely as 'this reduces our technical debt.' Translate this into business-case vocabulary a CFO would find credible.
drills.a: Quantify current cost (engineer-hours/month spent working around it, incident cost attributable to it), state investment required, express as payback period (months to recoup via reduced maintenance/incident cost) with a stated confidence range rather than a bare technical claim.

drills.q: Why does a risk-adjusted range with stated confidence and source beat a single confident point estimate in a business case?
drills.a: Finance reviewers are trained to distrust suspiciously precise, unsourced numbers. A range with a named basis survives scrutiny because you can defend where it came from; a fabricated precise number collapses the moment someone asks its source.

drills.q: You've made your case, been heard, and been overruled. What's the senior move, and why does it matter for future decisions?
drills.a: State disagreement once, clearly, then execute the decision fully -- no relitigating or passive undermining. Credibility is a finite, reputational resource; being known for accepting a loss badly means less benefit of the doubt on the next disagreement, which might matter more.

drills.q: Design the smallest possible 'yes' to ask for when a Decider is hesitant to commit to a large, uncertain proposal.
drills.a: Identify the single riskiest assumption underlying the big decision, propose a time-boxed pilot targeting just that assumption, with a defined checkpoint and explicit kill criteria -- this asks the Decider to risk far less than the full commitment while generating real evidence either way.

drills.q: What's the 'how did you get there' technique and when is it more effective than arguing directly against a decision you disagree with?
drills.a: Asking the decision-maker to walk through their reasoning surfaces information or constraints you may not have, avoiding an argument against a strawman of their actual position. Most effective when you suspect they have context you're missing (budget, other stakeholders, political factors) -- common in real organizations.

drills.q: A peer team lead objects that their use case is 'different enough' that your proposed shared infrastructure won't fit. How do you determine if this is a real technical objection or resistance to losing control, and why does it matter which?
drills.a: Use the 'how did you get there' technique to understand the specific concern in detail rather than assuming either explanation. If real, your design needs an actual extension point to address it -- dismissing a genuine technical objection as politics costs credibility. If it turns out to be more about autonomy than fit, that's a different, harder conversation about incentives that a better technical pitch alone won't resolve.

drills.q: When should you NOT spend your influence capital trying to change a decision, even if you disagree with it?
drills.a: When the decision is small and easily reversible (low cost of being wrong), when your own confidence in your position isn't actually high, or when you've already spent significant capital recently elsewhere -- influence capital is finite and reputational, and spending it indiscriminately depletes it for the decision that matters most.
